title: Emptiness in each school
hookLine: not-self in the Pali texts, emptiness in the Mahayana: related, differently stressed

cards: Ananda, the Buddha's attendant, asks him a plain question in the Pali texts. People say the world is empty. In what way is it empty?
It's the kind of question a friend asks on a long walk, and the Buddha gives a plain answer: the world is empty of a self, and of anything belonging to a self.
The eye, the forms it sees, the thoughts that follow: none of them is a self you could own. Later, Mahayana teachers would build a great deal on that one word, empty.

teach.b: First, not-self in the Pali texts, which you met back in year one. In one talk, the Buddha takes the body, feelings, perceptions, mental formations and consciousness one at a time.
If the body were a self, he says, it wouldn't lead to affliction; you could tell it, let my body be this way, and it would obey. It doesn't. So it isn't a self.
The Pali word is anatta. The weight falls on persons: the bundle you call me, seen through, so clinging loosens. Second, emptiness in the Mahayana.

teach.h: EVERY THING EMPTY OF FIXED NATURE.
teach.b: The Perfection of Wisdom sutras, and the short one people chant, the Heart Sutra, widen the word: not just the person but every thing, every quality, even the teachings themselves, are empty of a fixed, independent nature.
One line, in paraphrase: form is emptiness, and emptiness is form. Third, Nagarjuna's turn.
The Indian teacher Nagarjuna said that emptiness is simply dependent arising: things are empty because they come from causes and conditions, not because they don't exist at all.
Emptiness, he warned, is not a new thing to grab. Fourth, the stress. Theravada teachers also speak of all phenomena as not-self, and Mahayana teachers also teach not-self of the person.
What differs is where the weight lands: the person seen through, or everything seen through, including the seeing.

how: Theravada practitioners contemplate not-self in the body and mind during insight meditation, while Mahayana communities often chant the Heart Sutra and study emptiness through Nagarjuna's writings.

games.q: what does “emptiness in each school” mean?
o: the teaching that nothing in the world truly exists at all
a blank, peaceful mind that has stopped all of its thinking
not-self of persons, or of all things, weighted by each school

p: form is emptiness, emptiness is form

s: the word empty first appears in Mahayana texts
in the Pali texts, the Buddha tells Ananda the world is empty of a self.
Nagarjuna said emptiness means nothing exists
he said emptiness is dependent arising: things come from causes and conditions.
in the Pali talk on not-self, the body won't obey a command
if it were a self, it would not lead to affliction; it would obey.

games.q: a Theravada friend says 'not-self.' a Zen friend says 'emptiness.' they start to argue. what do you say?
o: one of you has it wrong.
it's related ground: the weight just lands in different places.
they have nothing to do with each other.
games.why: the Pali texts already say the world is empty of a self; the Mahayana widens emptiness to all things. same root, different stress.

practice: Wait for one sound to arrive, a car, a bird, the hum of a fridge, and as it comes and goes, note gently, the old Pali way: this is not mine to command.

Then, the Mahayana way, notice what the same sound leans on, air, ears, distance, attention, and let it be empty of standing alone. Notice one difference between the two, kindly, without crowning either.

wordCard.voice: Emptiness in each school. Not-self of the person in the Pali texts; the emptiness of all things in the Mahayana. Related teachings, differently stressed. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: differently stressed. Two ways of seeing through, one root beneath them. Until tomorrow.

drop.name: the schools side by side, never ranked
